q: The resolving power of an optical instrument describes its ability to:
o: Show two close objects as separate
Collect more light from a faint object
x: Resolving power is the ability to distinguish two nearby points or objects as separate; it is set by the minimum angle of resolution. Making things look larger is magnifying power, a different idea.

q: The same convex lens is used as a magnifying glass by the same person, once with the final image at the near point and once with the final image at infinity. The magnifying power at the near point is greater by:
x: With the image at the near point M = 1 + d/f, and with the image at infinity M = d/f. The difference is exactly 1, whatever the focal length.

q: A child whose near point is 15 cm and an adult whose near point is 30 cm each use a convex lens of focal length 5 cm as a magnifier, with the final image at their own near point. Their magnifying powers are:
o: 4 for the child and 7 for the adult
7 for the child and 4 for the adult
3 for the child and 6 for the adult
x: M = 1 + d/f: child 1 + 15/5 = 4, adult 1 + 30/5 = 7. Someone with a farther near point sees the object smaller without the lens, so the lens helps more. Using d/f alone gives 3 and 6.

q: A telescope objective of diameter 12.2 cm is used with light of wavelength 600 nm. Using α = 1.22 λ/D, what is the smallest distance between two craters on the Moon, 4 × 10⁸ m away, that it can just resolve?
x: α = 1.22 × 6 × 10⁻⁷/0.122 = 6 × 10⁻⁶ rad. Separation = α × distance = 6 × 10⁻⁶ × 4 × 10⁸ = 2.4 × 10³ m = 2.4 km. Leaving out the factor 1.22 gives about 2.0 km; taking D as 1.22 cm gives 24 km.

q: An insect 2 mm long is viewed with a magnifying glass of magnifying power 10. Without the lens it would be viewed at the near point, 25 cm away. What angle does its image subtend at the eye through the lens?
x: Unaided angle = 0.002 m/0.25 m = 0.008 rad. Magnifying power is the ratio of angles, so the image subtends 10 × 0.008 = 0.08 rad. Stopping at the unaided angle gives 0.008 rad.

q: A normal eye cannot see an object clearly when it is held closer than about 25 cm because:
o: The object then forms no image at all
The eye lens cannot be made any more converging to focus it
Light from close objects travels too slowly
x: To focus nearer objects the eye muscles make the eye lens more converging (accommodation). At the near point the lens has reached its greatest power, so closer objects form a blurred image.

q: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. In normal adjustment, its magnifying power and its length are:
x: In normal adjustment M = fₒ/fₑ = 100/5 = 20, and the lenses are separated by fₒ + fₑ = 105 cm. Subtracting the focal lengths gives 95 cm; multiplying them gives 500.

q: Compared with the objective of an astronomical telescope, the objective of a compound microscope has:
o: A long focal length and a large aperture
A long focal length and a small aperture
A short focal length and a small aperture
The same focal length but a larger aperture
x: A microscope objective is close to a tiny nearby object and must give a large real image, so it has a very short focal length and a small aperture. A telescope objective must collect light from distant objects and needs a long focal length and a wide aperture.

q: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. The eyepiece is adjusted so that the final image is at the near point, 25 cm from the eye held close to the eyepiece. What is the magnifying power?
x: For the eyepiece, 1/u = 1/5 + 1/25 = 6/25, so the intermediate image is 25/6 cm from it. The angular magnification is fₒ/u = 100 × 6/25 = 24, the same as (fₒ/fₑ)(1 + fₑ/d) = 20 × 1.2. Using normal adjustment gives 20.

q: In a spectrometer, the telescope is used to:
o: Bring the parallel rays leaving the prism or grating to a focus at its cross-wires, so the spectrum can be viewed
Make the light from the slit into a parallel beam
Split white light into its colours
Hold the prism at the minimum deviation position
x: The collimator makes the light parallel, the prism or grating disperses it, and the telescope focuses each parallel beam of one colour into a sharp line at its cross-wires. Its angle is read on the circular scale.

q: An object is placed 1.1 cm from the objective of a compound microscope, whose focal length is 1 cm. What linear magnification does the objective produce?
x: 1/q = 1/f − 1/p = 1 − 1/1.1 = 0.1/1.1, so q = 11 cm and m = q/p = 11/1.1 = 10. Check: the object is 0.1 cm beyond the focus, and m = f/0.1 = 10. Taking the image distance itself as the magnification gives 11.

q: Compared with the object, the final image seen through a compound microscope is:
x: The objective forms a real, inverted, magnified image; the eyepiece acts as a magnifier on it and gives a virtual image, still inverted relative to the object and further magnified.

q: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. The eyepiece is changed so that the magnifying power in normal adjustment becomes 40. What is the new distance between the lenses?
x: M = fₒ/fₑ, so the new eyepiece has fₑ = 100/40 = 2.5 cm. In normal adjustment the length is fₒ + fₑ = 102.5 cm. Doubling the eyepiece focal length instead gives 110 cm.

q: In Michelson's rotating-mirror method, an eight-sided mirror is replaced by a sixteen-sided mirror, with the distant mirror at the same distance. For the image to be seen steadily, the mirror must now turn:
o: At a quarter of the rate
x: The image is steady when the mirror turns from one face to the next during the round-trip time. With 16 faces it must turn only 1/16 of a revolution in that same time instead of 1/8, so half the rate is enough.

q: In Michelson's method an eight-sided mirror rotates at 750 rev s⁻¹, and the image is steady when it turns one-eighth of a revolution during the light's round trip. Taking c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, how far away is the distant mirror?
x: Round-trip time t = 1/(8 × 750) = 1/6000 s. The light travels 2d = ct = 3 × 10⁸/6000 = 5 × 10⁴ m, so d = 25 km. Forgetting that the light goes there and back gives 50 km.

q: Doctors look inside a patient's stomach with an endoscope. The endoscope carries light and the image along:
o: A narrow hollow metal tube with mirrors
x: An endoscope uses flexible bundles of optical fibres: one bundle carries light in by total internal reflection, and a coherent bundle carries the image back out.

q: An advantage of an optical fibre over a copper cable for carrying telephone signals is that the fibre:
o: Can also carry electric power to the telephone
Is not affected by electrical interference from nearby circuits
Makes light travel faster than it does in air
Never needs any repeaters, however long it is
x: Signals in a fibre are light, so nearby electric and magnetic fields do not disturb them; fibres also carry far more information with less loss. Light is slower in glass than in air, and long links still need repeaters.

q: The core of an optical fibre has refractive index 1.60 and the cladding has refractive index 1.20. What is sin C, where C is the critical angle at the core-cladding boundary?
x: sin C = n(cladding)/n(core) = 1.20/1.60 = 0.75. Using 1/n(core), as for a core in air, gives 0.625; dividing the other way gives 1.33, which no sine can equal.
